title: Optically-Induced Modulation and Programming of Diamond Photonic Cavities
authors: Yuchun Zhu, Amirali Arabmoheghi, Nicolas Le Thomas, Niels Quack, Valentin Goblot, Christophe Galland
abstract: Single-crystal diamond combines exceptional optical, thermal, and mechanical properties while hosting optically addressable and spin-coherent colour centres, making it a promising platform for integrated quantum and nonlinear photonics. However, practical post-fabrication mechanisms for dynamically controlling and tuning monolithic diamond photonic circuits remain limited. Here, we demonstrate all-optical modulation and long-lived tuning of suspended diamond Fabry--Perot nanobeam cavities containing nitrogen-vacancy centres. Under 532~nm illumination, the infrared (1000 to 1100~nm) cavity response is governed by two competing contributions: a well-understood thermo-optic red-shift, and a novel charge-mediated blue-shift that we attribute to the free-carrier plasma dispersion effect. With 10~mW of 20~kHz-modulated green light, we achieve an infrared modulation depth of approximately 45\% of the available reflection contrast. Green illumination also produces quasi-permanent photo-refractive resonance blue-shifts, with a maximum observed tuning of 3.15~nm (0.87~THz), without measurable degradation of the cavity linewidth or contrast. Achieving the same cavity shift in a lithium-niobate Pockels modulator would require 200 to 500~V across a \(5~μ\mathrm{m}\) electrode gap. These results establish a monolithic diamond nanophotonic platform combining agile and reversible modulation with long-lived optical reconfiguration, two key ingredients in photonic technologies.
summary: This paper demonstrates a novel method to dynamically control and tune diamond photonic cavities using only light. By inducing both fast thermal shifts and slow, quasi-permanent charge-mediated blue-shifts, the authors establish a highly reconfigurable platform. This work is crucial for developing integrated quantum and nonlinear photonic technologies.
main_problem: The primary challenge addressed is developing practical, dynamic, and tunable mechanisms for controlling monolithic diamond photonic circuits.
main_result: The authors demonstrated all-optical modulation ($\approx 45\%$ depth) and long-lived, reversible tuning ($\Delta\lambda = 3.15 	ext{ nm}$) of diamond photonic cavities using green light excitation.
method: The study employed optical spectroscopy, using an IR laser to probe the cavity resonance while modulating or illuminating it with a green laser (532 nm) to induce changes.
model_or_system: The platform utilizes suspended diamond Fabry-Perot nanobeam cavities containing Nitrogen-Vacancy (NV) color centers. The physics involves competing contributions to the cavity shift: a thermo-optic red-shift and a novel charge-mediated blue-shift via free-carrier plasma dispersion.
key_observables: Infrared modulation depth, photo-refractive resonance blue-shift ($\Delta\lambda$), cavity linewidth, and time-dependent resonance shifts.
important_parameters: Modulation depth of $\approx 45\%$; maximum tuning of $3.15 	ext{ nm}$ ($0.87 	ext{ THz}$); comparison to high-voltage Pockels modulators.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the free-carrier response is governed by the Drude model and that the observed shifts are due to the combination of thermal and photo-carrier effects.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the experimental setup, long-lived photorefractive tuning over days, time-domain responses distinguishing fast thermal and slow charge-related shifts, and spectral analysis comparing different illumination conditions.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first demonstrating the feasibility of all-optical modulation and tuning, then analyzing the temporal dynamics to separate thermal and charge-related shifts, and finally performing detailed modeling to confirm the free-carrier mechanism over singlet absorption.
why_interesting: The work directly addresses the integration of quantum emitters (NV centers) into advanced photonic circuits, providing a platform for quantum light sources and nonlinear optics, which is central to quantum information processing.
